questions.q: What is the ITIL 4 purpose of the service request management practice?
options: To support the agreed quality of a service by handling all predefined, user-initiated service requests in an effective and user-friendly manner
To restore normal service operation as quickly as possible after an unplanned interruption
To find the root cause of recurring service disruptions
To assess and authorize proposed changes to the IT environment
questions.explain: Service request management exists to handle predefined, user-initiated asks — not to fix something broken, which is incident management's job.

questions.q: A user's laptop screen has gone completely black and won't turn on. Is this a service request?
options: Yes, because any user-initiated ticket counts as a service request
No, because the service is not working as designed — this is an unplanned interruption, which is an incident
Yes, because hardware problems always fall under service request management
It cannot be classified without first running a root cause analysis
questions.explain: A broken laptop is an unplanned interruption to a working service — that's the definition of an incident, not a service request.

questions.q: Why does ITIL 4 emphasize that service requests should be "predefined"?
options: Because predefined requests never require any approval step
Because predefining a request removes the need for a service catalog
So the approval chain and fulfillment steps are already designed in advance, making requests fast and consistent instead of improvised each time
Because only predefined requests are allowed to be logged as tickets
questions.explain: Predefining a request means the information needed, the approvers, and the fulfillment steps are already known, so the practice runs on repeatable workflows rather than ad hoc problem-solving.

questions.q: What role does a service catalog play in service request management?
options: It is where incidents are logged and prioritized by impact and urgency
It replaces the need for any approval workflow on high-risk requests
It is only used by the service desk, never by end users directly
It acts as the front door, listing exactly what can be requested and capturing the required information up front
questions.explain: A service catalog surfaces predefined requests to users, capturing details like cost center or approver at the point of request instead of through a vague back-and-forth.

questions.q: Why do some catalog requests, like a password reset, often skip a formal approval step entirely?
options: Because the service desk manually waives approval on a case-by-case basis for every request
Because the risk is low enough that pre-approval was already built into how the request was designed
Because low-risk requests are not considered real service requests
Because approval steps are only used for incidents, never for requests
questions.explain: Some predefined requests are designed to fulfill automatically or near-instantly because their risk was already judged low enough at design time, not because approval doesn't matter for requests in general.
